Statement II: Ubiquinone receives reducing equivalents from NADH through complex I and from FADH₂ through complex II.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Cytochrome c is a small protein attached to the outer surface of the inner membrane; it acts as a mobile carrier between complex III (cytochrome bc₁ complex) and complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase). Ubiquinone receives reducing equivalents from NADH via complex I and from FADH₂ via complex II; reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) is then oxidised by complex III.
steps: Statement I: false, cytochrome c links complex III and complex IV
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Respiration in Plants', Electron Transport System (ETS) and Oxidative Phosphorylation
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following is true of both lactic acid fermentation and alcoholic fermentation?

options.text: Both reoxidise the NADH + H⁺ formed in glycolysis to NAD⁺
Both take place in the mitochondrial matrix
Both release more energy per glucose than aerobic respiration

solution.explanation: In both lactic acid and alcoholic fermentation the reducing agent is NADH + H⁺, which is reoxidised to NAD⁺ as pyruvic acid is reduced. Alcoholic fermentation releases CO₂ (pyruvic acid → CO₂ + ethanol) but lactic acid fermentation does not. Both occur in the cytoplasm, and both release less than seven per cent of the energy in glucose.
solution.why_others_wrong: Lactic acid fermentation releases no CO₂. Fermentation is cytoplasmic. It releases far less energy than aerobic respiration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Respiration in Plants', Fermentation
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both reoxidise the NADH + H⁺ formed in glycolysis to NAD⁺

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text:
The oxygen supply to a respiring plant cell is completely cut off. Which of the following will stop or decrease?

(a) The flow of electrons through the electron transport system
(b) The continued oxidation of acetyl CoA in the TCA cycle
(c) Glycolysis
(d) The ATP yield per molecule of glucose
(e) The conversion of pyruvic acid to ethanol

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Consequences of the absence of oxygen
solution.explanation: Oxygen is the final hydrogen acceptor of the ETS, so without it electron flow stops. The TCA cycle needs continued regeneration of NAD⁺ and FAD⁺ from NADH and FADH₂ in the ETS, so it also stops. Glycolysis does not need oxygen and continues, with NAD⁺ regenerated by fermentation, so pyruvic acid is converted to products such as ethanol. Since only glycolysis yields ATP, the ATP yield per glucose falls.
solution.why_others_wrong: Each wrong combination includes glycolysis or ethanol formation, which continue without oxygen, or leaves out a step that stops.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Respiration in Plants', Fermentation; Electron Transport System (ETS) and Oxidative Phosphorylation
solution.final_answer: Option D: (a), (b) and (d) only

questions.subject: Botany
questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria from photophosphorylation in chloroplasts?

options.text: In oxidative phosphorylation light energy creates the proton gradient, whereas in photophosphorylation the energy of oxidation-reduction is used
Only photophosphorylation uses an ATP synthase to make ATP
In oxidative phosphorylation the energy of oxidation-reduction is used to create the proton gradient, whereas in photophosphorylation light energy is used
Only oxidative phosphorylation requires a proton gradient across a membrane

solution.explanation: NCERT points out that in photophosphorylation light energy is used to produce the proton gradient needed for phosphorylation, while in respiration the energy of oxidation-reduction is used for the same purpose; hence the name oxidative phosphorylation. Both use a proton gradient across a membrane and an ATP synthase.
steps: Source of energy for the gradient: redox (mitochondria) vs light (chloroplasts)

solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Respiration in Plants', Electron Transport System (ETS) and Oxidative Phosphorylation
solution.final_answer: Option C: In oxidative phosphorylation the energy of oxidation-reduction is used to create the proton gradient, whereas in photophosphorylation light energy is used
